sources.citation: Heine, Bernd & Henry Honken. 2010. The Kx'a family: a new Khoisan genealogy. Journal of Asian and African Studies 79: 5-36.

sources.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2004. What African languages tell us about accent typology. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 37: 101-136.
sources.note: Family-level, second-hand: 'All the Khoisan languages are described as having tone, and I could find no discussion of stress in the existing Khoisan literature.' (sec. 4). Nothing specific to !Xun of Angola.

sources.citation: Bleek, Dorothea F. 1956. A Bushman Dictionary (American Oriental Series 41). New Haven: American Oriental Society. [NIII = !O!kung of Angola]
sources.note: No word-stress statement (grep stress/accent/emphasis). Letter-B note: 'Among the !o !kun of Angola b has a tendency to slide into v'. Under N/NG a general all-Bushman remark that nasals are 'frequently found in unstressed second syllables and at the end of words' -- not a stress rule and not NIII-specific.

sources.citation: Bleek, Dorothea F. 1928. Bushmen of Central Angola. Bantu Studies 3(2): 105-125 (LANGUAGE paragraph p.125).

sources.note: Nothing. Ethnographic travel report; linguistic content = a Mbunda (Bantu) noun-class table, personal names, and the paragraph 'Sprachveränderung' (p.56) on young men dropping initial clicks and Nyemba loans. Only 'Ton' hit is a musical-bow pitch remark (p.53).
